California Says Uber Driver Is Employee, Not a Contractor

Their argument that the drivers are treated like employees and thus should be counted as employees doesn't make a lot of sense to me. Tons of companies hire contractors for things like software development and construction. Those people are expected to work certain hours, dress appropriately and act in the same manner as an employee. Why are they still contractors when and Uber driver who isn't required to work specific hours isn't a contractor?
Uber controls the fares and the driver's cut and Uber decides what cars can be used and when to fire poorly rated drivers. These are factors taken into account of the whole and the business model.

But can't parallel things be said for all contractors? If a construction contractor does a bad job framing something, they will get fired. If they don't bring proper tools, they can't work. Most construction contractors have to bring their own basic tools for a job and if they can't provide the tools, they won't be given work.

Note: I am not a labor/employment lawyer so I'm enjoying trying to make sense of it all as well, but (1) if an independent contractor doesn't bring proper tools but still does the job correctly (and within timeframes) no, that isn't a reason to fire an independent contractor unless specific provisions are written into the contract... that contractor would immediately sue for breach of contract and win. Something like forcing specific tools or requiring set hours (in this case a level of vehicle) weighs heavily on whether that person is an employee.

(2) The analogy is more like a construction contractor's employee. A person owning a house, for example, hires a construction contractor. That relationship would, presumably, be that of an independent contractor. But that contractor has employees of its own, presumably those who have restrictions set for how they can and can't do their job. That relationship is employer/employee. If a person seeking to hire a driver has to go through Uber to hire a specific driver, it definitely leans more in favor of the concept that those drivers are Uber employees.

(3) I do not exactly know how the concept of Uber's percentage take is involved, but I have a strong feeling that taking a cut, especially if large, weighs in Uber's favor.

(4) The continuity of their employment is also surely an issue. They aren't hired for one job (i.e. construct this house). They are asked to be continuously on call for the company.

I'm not any sort of lawyer either. I judt don't understand this ruling. On point 1, I totally see where you're coming from and I agree. But with a hospitality based company like Uber, the quality of the car is a part of the experience and thus a refelection fo the quality of the product. So an inferiorer car could constitute not doing the job properly.

 

point 2 is something that I hadn't thought of. I completely agree with it. It makes total sense that I'm contracting Uber and Uber is using it's employees to fulfill the task. Since I'm not in direct contact with the driver, Uber is the entity that I'm contracting for a ride not the driver himself. Where I could see a hole in this is that Uber is contracting it's drivers on a per-ride basis. The obvious hole in that though is the barrier to entry for being a driver. The work required to become a driver and get set up with uber is comparable to that of an employee relationship.

 

For 3, I'm equally in the dark so I'm not going to try to argue one way or another.

 

For 4 though, I was under the impression that Uber does not keep people on call. That's why rates vary. They increase the fare when there aren't enough drivers on the road to convince drivers to get out and drive. In that respect, the employment is completely at will from the driver's side. If a driver choses not to drive, they recieve no fairs. But since Uber didn't promise a set number of fairs or require specific working hours, they aren't in the wrong if a driver chooses not to work. If a driver's work schedule is entirely his/her choosing, that seems much more like a contractee relashionship.
